Isolation between runs relies on that user's state per run: other clones and earlier transcripts are moved out of its reach or deleted before the next invocation. No container and no second machine. A real OS-enforced boundary for the benchmark checkout and the hidden requirements, independent of the program under test, on the machine the maintainer already has and without touching Docker. All runs share one user, so keeping one run from reading another's clone or transcript depends on per-run cleanup and on runs not overlapping, which ties it to the concurrent-runs sibling; the harness needs privilege escalation to switch users, and the user's tools, browsers, and credentials must be provisioned separately on a machine that also does daily work.

Confinement: one fresh container per run on the development Mac, through a container runtime other than Docker Desktop's (or Docker Desktop itself, if a check shows the recorded blocker concerns only the host's own shell sandbox and not a containerized headless invocation). The container mounts only that run's clone read-write and the plugin checkout read-only, has its own home so its projects directory is its own, and is discarded after the run; the harness and the operator stay outside it on the Mac. Each run sees only its clone by construction, so the benchmark checkout, sibling clones, and other runs' transcripts are all out of reach regardless of what the agent tries or how runs overlap, while the campaign stays on the maintainer's own machine. Rests on an untested premise, that the Docker Desktop blocker does not extend to a container runtime on this Mac; the run then executes on a Linux image rather than macOS, so the image becomes an input whose OS, tools, and browsers must be stated (the execution-environment sibling's axis), and the host's credentials must be passed into each container.

Confinement: one fresh container per run, as in the Mac container option (only the clone read-write, the plugin checkout read-only, a container-own home and projects directory, discarded after the run), executed on a dedicated Linux machine or Linux VM rather than the development Mac. The harness, the benchmark checkout, and the operator run on that host outside the containers; the Mac only starts campaigns and reads results. Strong per-run isolation on a platform where the container and shell-sandbox tooling is known to work, sidestepping the Docker Desktop blocker entirely and leaving the maintainer's machine and configuration out of every run. Needs a Linux machine to be provisioned, paid for or maintained, and kept as a stated environment for the whole campaign, plus the host's credentials on it; nothing in the project has run there yet, so the draft commits to infrastructure that exists only on paper.

Confinement: a whole virtual machine per run. The harness, kept on a controller (the Mac or a server), creates a fresh VM (a cloud instance or a hosted CI runner job) holding only the run's clone, the plugin checkout, and the host binary, drives every invocation in it remotely, collects the outputs and the branch, and destroys the VM; the benchmark checkout and the operator never exist on the run's machine. The strongest boundary on offer: nothing of the benchmark, other runs, or any shared configuration is present on the machine where the agent works, and each run's environment starts from the same image, which also helps reproducibility on another machine. The most infrastructure and the slowest per run: image building, remote control, credential handling per VM, and per-run machine cost, all of it a harness the draft must specify before a single run; a hosted CI runner also ties execution to that service's limits and images.

open-question.question: Nothing states what OS, tools on PATH, and browsers a run finds, though these shape what every scenario can build and what the rater can drive. Is the execution environment declared as a versioned shared input of a comparison set, recorded in the manifest only, or left unrecorded?
open-question.alternative: The run environment (OS and version, the tools on PATH with their versions, the installed browsers) is written as one environment definition under the inputs area, versioned by content under an id like the operator definition, and listed among the shared inputs; the pre-flight probes the live machine and refuses the run when it does not match the definition, the manifest records the definition's id, and a change to the definition starts a new comparison set. The run agent is told nothing beyond what the seed's CLAUDE.md already says, and the rater's browser stays in the rater definition as now. Puts the environment under the same rule as every other input that shapes results (byte-identical across scenarios, recorded by content, a change never mixed into a comparison), and gives a later re-run on another machine a target it can be checked against rather than a guess. Every probed version has to be held still for a whole campaign, so auto-updating browsers and tools must be pinned or disabled and a drifted machine refuses runs until reprovisioned; whether the pin can be enforced depends on the machine and confinement the filesystem-reach question settles, and whether a change starts a new set rests on the axis the comparison-set-definition question owns.

The environment is declared inside the seed's CLAUDE.md, which the draft already calls an environment description: it names the OS, the tools on PATH, and the browsers a run finds, so the seed tag versions the declaration and no separate input or manifest field is added; the pre-flight probes the machine against the same list and refuses on a mismatch, and a change to the environment is a change to the seed and starts a new comparison set through the seed tag. The run agent reads the declaration; the rater's browser stays in the rater definition. Adds no new kind of input and no new versioning path, and every scenario learns equally what it can use (for example that no package manager is present), so no run spends turns discovering the machine or builds against a tool that is absent. Any environment change, even a browser patch release, bumps the seed tag, which invalidates every phase-1 run as a parent for phase 2 and moves the trend's seed line; and telling the agent which tools exist shapes what each scenario builds, turning a measurement condition into part of the prompt every run reads.

The environment is declared as an environment definition under the inputs area, as a provisioning target rather than a set-defining input; the harness probes the live machine at the manifest step and records the observed OS, PATH tool versions, and browsers in an environment field of the manifest beside the definition's id, and a mismatch with the definition is flagged by the analysis step and reported beside the affected rows rather than refusing the run or starting a new comparison set. The run agent is told nothing new; the rater's browser stays in the rater definition. Gives another machine a stated target to reproduce while letting a campaign that spans days absorb a browser or tool auto-update without discarding the set, with every deviation visible in the record instead of hidden. A flagged mismatch still sits inside one comparison, so a difference between scenarios can be partly the environment's, against the rule that a difference is attributed only to what differs between definitions; the analysis must decide per flag whether it matters, which is a judgment the rest of the design avoids. Whether drift may stay inside a set is the axis the comparison-set-definition question owns.

No environment is declared. The harness probes the live machine at the manifest step and records what it finds (OS and version, a fixed list of tools on PATH with their versions, installed browsers) in an environment field of each run's manifest; the environment is not a shared input, a change starts no new comparison set, and the analysis may group or compare runs by the recorded values after the fact. The rater's browser stays in the rater definition. Costs one probe and one manifest field, needs no provisioning or pinning, and still leaves a record from which any later question about what a run found can be answered. Records without controlling: runs on two machines or across an update mix silently within a set unless someone reads the field, a later re-run has nothing to reproduce but a list of observed versions, and the fixed probe list misses any tool a run reached that the list did not name.

The environment is neither declared nor recorded: a run finds whatever the machine running the harness has, and the draft states this choice with its reason (all scenarios of a campaign run on one machine, so the environment is common to them) instead of leaving it unsaid. Nothing to build, pin, or maintain, and within one campaign on one unchanged machine every scenario does meet the same environment. Results cannot be reproduced or audited elsewhere, and a tool or browser update during a campaign, or a move to another machine (which the filesystem-reach question may require), changes what scenarios can build with no trace, mixed into the trend as if it were a plugin change.

open-question.question: A Cairn skill that stops on its own precondition prints a message and exits 0, so the harness, which stops the chain only on a non-zero exit, carries on past it and can record a chain that closed an empty milestone as every invocation made. By what signal does the harness detect that an invocation stopped on a skill's own check rather than completing?

Each skill's success line is fixed and identifier-free, but apart from the bootstrap's no-op line the no-op and precondition-stop messages are prose whose wording the files only exemplify, so a harness matching final messages can recognize success but not which stop occurred. Does Cairn fix the wording of every skill's no-op and stop lines in this milestone?
open-question.alternative: Cairn's skills are not changed in this milestone. Every no-op and stop message keeps its current form: prose whose wording the SKILL.md files only exemplify, with the bootstrap's `Workflow already bootstrapped — nothing changed.` the one fixed exception. The draft states that a harness can recognize only the fixed success lines, so any final message that is not one counts as "not a success", with which stop it was left unclassified or read by hand from the run record. The fix is left for a later Cairn milestone, or never made. No runtime file, host rebuild, or test changes. The draft already keeps where a chain stopped as unscored record read by hand, and success against non-success is enough to find the first invocation that did not complete. The manifest cannot say which stop ended a chain (a derive refusal, an empty task list, a no-op finish), so telling a behavioural stop from a model's improvised message needs a person. Whether this is enough depends on the signal the sibling stop-detection question settles on. The same prose stop can also be worded differently from run to run, which weakens comparison across runs.

Every skill's no-op and stop messages open with one of a small fixed set of identifier-free class prefixes, for example one for "nothing changed" and one for "stopped on a precondition". The rest of the line, and any lines after it, stay free prose, including variable detail such as Short Titles or a tool's `Error:` line. Each SKILL.md's reporting step states the prefix, and the set is listed once in `docs/skill-reference.md`. Nothing tests that the prefixes appear. A small, uniform edit across all skills that lets a harness sort each final message into success, no-op, or stop with one match, without fixing dozens of individual lines. The harness can tell that a stop happened but not which one, so the question's aim of recognizing which stop occurred is only half met. Nothing catches a later edit that drops or rewords a prefix.

The same fixed class prefixes as above, on every skill's no-op and stop messages, with free prose after them. They are also pinned by a test in the pytest suite that reads the rendered skill files and fails when a reporting step no longer carries its listed prefix, or when the list in `docs/skill-reference.md` drifts from the skill files. The success / no-op / stop sorting becomes a checked contract that a benchmark harness can depend on across Cairn versions, at the cost of a single small test. It still cannot say which stop occurred. It also adds a test that scrapes runtime prose, a kind of check the suite has so far kept only for the answer sweep's fixed shell calls, and every later change to a reporting step must keep that test passing.

Only the skills the draft's chains invoke get fixed wording: bootstrap, define, goto, starting-state, review, the two annotating passes, the answer skills and sweep, derive, complete-all-tasks, and finish. Each distinct no-op and precondition-stop condition in them gets its own fixed, identifier-free first line, unique across the plugin. Variable detail (the titles derive-tasks lists, the sweep's stopped-at Short Title, a quoted `Error:` line) moves to the lines after it. The lines are listed in `docs/skill-reference.md`. Skills outside the chains keep example wording, and nothing tests the lines. A harness matching final messages can name exactly which stop ended a chain. The edit is limited to the skills the benchmark actually exercises, which keeps this milestone's runtime change and its rebuild bounded. The plugin ends up with two reporting conventions, one for chain skills and one for the rest, so a skill that later joins a chain needs the same work redone. Nothing guards the fixed lines against drift, so a later wording edit silently breaks the harness's classification.

The same scope and form as the chain-skills option: a fixed, unique, identifier-free first line for each no-op and precondition stop in the chain skills, with variable detail on later lines and the list in `docs/skill-reference.md`. A pytest test also checks each listed line verbatim against the rendered skill files and checks that no two stops share a line. Skills outside the chains keep example wording. Exact stop identification for every skill the benchmark runs, as a contract checked on every commit, so a harness built against one Cairn version keeps classifying correctly on the next. The work stays limited to the chain skills. Two reporting conventions remain. The new prose-scraping test must be maintained, and it fails on any rewording of a chain skill's stop step, which slows ordinary edits to those skills.

Every skill in the plugin, inside and outside the chains (capture, submit-task, complete-task, modify-milestone-goal, and the rest included), gets a fixed, unique, identifier-free first line for each distinct no-op and precondition-stop condition, with variable detail on the lines after it. The lines are listed in `docs/skill-reference.md`, and the CLAUDE.md terse-reporting invariant is extended from success lines to them. Nothing tests the lines. One uniform reporting rule across the whole plugin, matching the existing fixed-success-line invariant, so every stop in any chain, present or future, can be identified by its line. The largest runtime edit of the prose options, touching every SKILL.md's reporting step and requiring a host rebuild, most of it for skills no benchmark chain runs. Nothing guards the lines against drift.

Every skill gets a fixed, unique, identifier-free first line for each distinct no-op and precondition-stop condition, with variable detail after it. The lines are listed in `docs/skill-reference.md`, and the CLAUDE.md terse-reporting invariant is extended to them. A pytest test checks each listed line verbatim against the rendered skill files and checks that every line is unique. The complete, checked contract: any final message of any skill can be classified exactly, and a rewording cannot reach a release without the test failing. The most work in this milestone: every reporting step is edited, the hosts are rebuilt, and a new prose-scraping test is added and must be maintained. It also turns reporting wording across the whole plugin into a frozen interface that every later skill edit must respect, largely for the benefit of one benchmark harness.

open-question.question: finish-current-milestone closes a milestone whenever TASKS_TODO.md holds no section, so a chain whose derivation line refused to run finishes an empty milestone, clears the pointer, and leaves a tree that looks like a completed chain. Should the finish skill refuse to close a milestone that recorded no completed task?

An early stop is counted as a result, which also covers a usage limit, an API overload, or a network error reaching an invocation as a failed call, and Cairn spends the most tokens so is the likeliest to hit them. What does the harness do with an invocation that ends in an infrastructure failure rather than in the model's own stop?

No scenario invocation carries a time or turn limit while the rater has one, so a runaway session can hold a run open indefinitely. Does each invocation get a time or turn limit, and how is an invocation that hits it classified?
open-question.alternative: Scenario invocations keep running with no time, turn, or spend limit, per invocation or per run, as the draft's one-run procedure now stands. A session ends only by itself or by a failed call, its wall-clock duration is recorded in the manifest as today, and no limit-hit end class exists. Adds no parameter to the design and cuts no scenario short. A slow invocation, most likely Cairn's long task-completion line, can never be stopped by a ceiling set too low, so no score depends on where the ceiling was set. A runaway or hung session holds its run, and any campaign waiting behind it, open indefinitely. The only way to end it is a person killing the process, which breaks the draft's rule that nothing about a run is done by hand, and the kill leaves an end that no rule classifies.

The harness kills each claude -p process after a fixed wall-clock ceiling. This covers the first-form invocation and each operator-reply resume, each process timed on its own. The ceiling is set generously, well above the longest normal invocation (for example a stated multiple of a pilot's longest), and declared as a shared input of the comparison set. A kill stops the chain and is recorded in the manifest as its own end class (time limit). The run is then scored like any other early stop: a result, rated on the tree it left. Bounds every run with one harness-side mechanism that needs no host flag and catches hangs as well as loops. It rarely binds, so it does not shape scores, and it fits the draft's existing rule that an early stop is a result, not a failed measurement. Wall-clock time also depends on API speed and the network, so a hit can come from a stalled connection rather than the model, and counting it as a result scores an outside slowdown against the scenario. Cairn's long invocations are the most exposed to this.

The same generous per-process wall-clock ceiling, declared as a shared input of the comparison set and enforced by the harness, but a kill is classified as an infrastructure failure, not a behavioural stop. It is recorded under that end class and handled by whatever the benchmark does with infrastructure failures, so it is not scored as the scenario's result. A scenario is not penalised for a session held open by something outside the model, such as a stalled API or network. That keeps the bias the gaps report raises (Cairn, the heaviest spender, being the likeliest to hit external limits) out of the scores. A genuine model runaway, such as a loop that never converges, also gets treated as an infrastructure failure, which hides a real behavioural failure mode and can reward it with a retry. What a hit costs depends on the axis the infrastructure-failure question owns.

alternative.id: Spend or turn cap as result

open-question.alternative: Each invocation runs under a fixed cap the host enforces in the model's own terms: a dollar budget (claude -p's --max-budget-usd) or a cap on agentic turns where the host offers one. The cap is set generously and declared as a shared input of the comparison set, and there is no wall-clock ceiling. Reaching the cap is a behavioural early stop, recorded in the manifest under a limit end class and rated on the tree left. A cap counted in spend or turns does not depend on API or network speed, so a hit always reflects what the model did. Classifying it as a result is then sound. It is also one parameter that is easy to state and to reproduce. It does not bound a hang that spends nothing, such as a stalled connection or a blocked tool call, so the indefinitely-open run the question raises remains possible. It also depends on a host flag whose scope over dispatched subagents must be confirmed, and that flag is recorded per host rather than enforced by the harness.

Two generous limits per claude -p process, both declared as shared inputs of the comparison set. The first is a host-enforced spend or turn cap; reaching it is a behavioural early stop, recorded and rated on the tree left. The second is a harness wall-clock ceiling set above anything the spend cap allows in normal operation; a kill there is classified as an infrastructure failure and handled by the infrastructure-failure policy. The manifest records which limit ended the invocation. Sorts the two ways a session runs away by mechanism, not by judgment: a model that keeps working hits the spend cap and is scored, and a session that stalls hits the clock and is not. This bounds every run without scoring outside slowdowns against a scenario. Two parameters to set, declare, and justify instead of one, plus a dependence on a host flag whose coverage of subagents must be confirmed. Handling of the clock hit depends on the axis the infrastructure-failure question owns.

A deliberately tight per-invocation limit, in time or spend, that is the same for every scenario and chosen to bind rather than to catch only runaways. Reaching it is an early stop rated on the tree left, so the benchmark measures quality reached within a fixed resource budget. Answers the question of which approach does best when given the same resources, a comparison a reader can take at face value without weighing cost separately. Turns the cost the draft reports beside quality into a constraint on quality. The draft states that Cairn is expected to cost more and that the benchmark reports by how much, so this would systematically cut Cairn's heaviest lines short and score that against it, and the scores would then depend on where the budget was set.

A single wall-clock ceiling on the whole run (every invocation, reply, and operator turn of one prompt's chain), declared as a shared input of the comparison set, with no per-invocation limit. When the deadline passes the harness kills the running process and stops the chain. The run is recorded with a deadline end class and rated on the tree left as an early stop. One number bounds every run's total duration, and with it the length of a campaign, without having to size a ceiling for each kind of invocation. Chains differ greatly in length, from the single manual message to Cairn's eleven or more lines, so one deadline either binds Cairn or is slack for manual. It also lets a runaway early invocation use up the time of every later line, so the stop shows up at a line that did nothing wrong.

open-question.question: A new rating writes new browser tests for every checklist line, so two ratings of one artifact can test the same line at different strictness, and the draft's claim that a second rating gets the same number holds only for re-running an existing test. What must a rater version pass before it may rate a comparison set, and what is the acceptance rule?

The lost count compares two independent ratings, the parent's and the child's, so rater noise shows as lines lost or gained when nothing changed, and no agreement figure is reported anywhere. Is a sample of each comparison set's artifacts rated twice with the agreement reported beside the scores, and at what sample size?
open-question.alternative: No artifact is rated twice and no agreement figure is computed. The draft's claim under "The axes" that a second rating of the same artifact gets the same number is narrowed to re-running a committed test, and the lost count is described as a tally that includes rater noise, a lost line being a pointer to the run record and never evidence on its own. Rater variability is left to whatever the rater version must pass before rating and to how precisely each checklist line is specified. Costs no extra rater run and adds nothing to the harness, the rating file, the analysis, or the page, while making the draft stop claiming a repeatability nobody measured. The lost count, the number phase 2 is expected to show Cairn's margin on, stays uninterpretable: a reader cannot tell whether a mean of two lost lines is behaviour or noise, and a rater version that drifts between ratings goes unnoticed. How much this costs depends on how strict the sibling rater calibration gate and checklist line specifications turn out to be.

The harness re-rates a fixed number of randomly chosen artifacts per prompt in each comparison set (for example five), as a fresh blind rating under the same rater version, the rater not told it is a repeat. Scores and the lost count use the first rating only. The analysis output reports the per-line verdict agreement (the share of lines with the same verdict in both ratings) and the per-axis score difference for the sample; the README page carries nothing new. Gives a developer a measured noise floor for every comparison set at a small, fixed rater cost that does not grow with the scenario roster or the number of runs. A sample this small yields a wide estimate and may miss the artifacts hardest to rate (a canvas UI, an unusual entry structure), and a reader of the page, where the ranking and the lost column are read, never sees the figure.

One randomly chosen run of every scenario, for each prompt, is re-rated blind under the same rater version, so the sample grows with the roster; scores use the first rating only. The per-line verdict agreement and the per-axis score difference are reported in one line beside the README ranking table, and the lost column carries a noise floor beside the mean lost count: the expected number of lines lost by rater disagreement alone, computed from the rate at which a line passing in one rating of an artifact fails in the other. No threshold is applied; a low agreement is published as it is. Puts the noise figure where the scores and the lost count are read, so a reader compares the lost count to what noise alone produces, and every scenario contributes, so an artifact style one delivery tends to produce cannot escape the sample. Rater cost grows with the roster, one repeat per scenario per prompt still gives a coarse per-scenario estimate, and the page gains one more figure to explain. Its size depends on the sibling scenario roster and runs-per-scenario decisions.

The per-scenario repeat sample and the page reporting of the per-scenario option, plus a declared minimum agreement (for example a per-line verdict agreement under which the set fails) that is part of the rater definition. A comparison set whose sample falls below it is not complete: its page is not regenerated, and it is rated again under a revised rater version. Turns the agreement figure into a guarantee: no comparison set reaches the page with a rater whose ratings demonstrably did not reproduce on that set's own artifacts, which a calibration set of reference artifacts cannot show. The threshold is a number nobody can derive and must be argued for, a failing set costs a full re-rating and can stall a campaign, and the gate overlaps the sibling rater calibration gate, so its value depends on what that gate already requires before a rater version may rate.

Every run id gets two independent blind ratings under the same rater version. A line's score is the mean of its two verdicts, the agreement per scenario and per axis is reported beside the scores on the page, and a prompt-1 line counts as lost only when both ratings of the parent pass it and both ratings of the child fail it. Halves the effect of single-rating noise on every score and makes the lost count robust by construction, with an agreement figure for every scenario rather than an estimate from a sample. Doubles the rating cost and time of every comparison set and of every development check, which the fast loop under "How Cairn development uses the benchmark" was built to keep at one rater run per candidate commit, and a line with split verdicts scores a half that no test can re-derive.

No random sample is drawn. Every line the analysis sorts as lost (and as gained) between a parent and its child is re-rated afresh on both artifacts, with a new test for that line only, and counts as lost only when the re-rating confirms both verdicts. The confirmation rate is reported beside the lost count; the axis scores carry no agreement figure. Spends rater runs only on the number the question names, so the published lost count holds only differences that reproduced, at a cost proportional to how many lines changed rather than to the size of the set. Measures noise only where a verdict already changed, so a line falsely kept or falsely failed on both artifacts is never caught, the confirmation re-rating removes false losses without finding missed ones, and the axis scores, which rank the scenarios, get no noise figure at all.

The per-scenario repeat sample with its agreement line and noise floor beside the README table, and in addition the targeted re-rating of every lost and gained line on both parent and child, a line counting as lost only when the re-rating confirms it. Covers both halves of the problem: the axis scores get a measured agreement figure on the page, and the lost count is both confirmed line by line and set against a noise floor. The most harness and analysis work of any partial option, two separate repeat mechanisms to specify and keep in step, and a rater cost that grows with both the roster and the number of changed lines; its size depends on the sibling scenario roster and runs-per-scenario decisions.

open-question.question: Each checklist line names a behaviour and nothing more, so a weak test (an undo button exists) and a strict one (the award is actually reversed) both satisfy it. Does each line carry a short specification of the case its test must drive and what it must assert?
open-question.alternative: Every test line (prompt 1's six stated and thirteen implied lines, prompt 2's stated line and eleven implied lines, and prompt 2's carry-between-profiles hidden line) gets a short specification written now into the draft's project section beside the line. The specification names the case the test must drive the artifact into and the observable outcome it must assert, stated as an outcome rather than a means, so the "any way through counts" rule still holds: for the award line, award a point, take it back, and assert the score is back to its earlier value, with a confirmation that prevents the award counting as well. The specification becomes part of the checklist, which stays derived from the draft and nothing else, and keeps the line's id. Pins the strictness of every test line at the one source the checklist is already derived from, so two ratings of one artifact test the same case with the same assertion and the specs are reviewed in the open within this milestone. Roughly thirty-two specs have to be written and agreed now, which lengthens the project section considerably, and an outcome stated too narrowly can fail a legitimate way through that the line's wording meant to accept.

alternative.id: Spec form in draft, specs at implementation

open-question.alternative: The draft adds the rule that every test line carries a specification of the case to drive and the outcome to assert, gives its form and one or two worked examples, and changes the derivation rule so the checklist is the draft's lines plus specifications authored in the benchmark repository's inputs area when the checklist is first built. The per-line specifications are not written in this milestone. Settles the design point (each line carries a spec) within the milestone's goal of finalizing the draft, without writing every spec before the harness, the rater, and an artifact to try them on exist. The checklist stops being derived from the draft alone, and until the specs are written nothing pins strictness; whether they are fixed before scored runs depends on the input-freeze question.

The checklist lines stay behaviour-only as the draft has them; each test line's specification of the case to drive and the outcome to assert lives in the rater definition, beside its fixed rating guideline, so it is part of the rater version that every rating file names and the analysis groups by. A sharpened or corrected spec is a new rater version, never a change to the checklist, so line ids and the checklist's derivation stay untouched and ratings made under different specs never mix. What a line means is split across two inputs, and a spec change regroups every earlier rating under an older rater version rather than being re-rated against the same checklist; how a rater version is gated depends on the rater-calibration question.

Only the test lines where a weak and a strict test plainly diverge (an award taken back, a reload surviving, a skip keeping its place, a tie settled, edits not lost, the carry between profiles) get a short case-and-assertion specification in the draft's project section; the remaining lines stay behaviour-only. Spends the writing where the variance actually arises and keeps lines whose test has one obvious form, such as the file opening from disk, as short as they are. Choosing which lines are ambiguous is itself a judgment, so a weak test the selection did not foresee still passes on an unspecified line.

alternative.id: One strictness rule in the guideline

open-question.alternative: No per-line specification. The rater's fixed rating guideline gains one general rule applied to every test line: a test must drive the artifact into the case the line names and assert the resulting state, never only the presence of a control, label, or button. Closes the named failure (a test that only finds an undo button) with one sentence that also covers lines added later, at no cost to the checklist's length. Leaves to each rating what the resulting state is for each line, so two strict tests can still assert different outcomes and disagree on the same artifact.

Nothing is added to the checklist lines or the rating guideline; a line keeps naming a behaviour only, and variance in test strictness is left to be caught by whatever checks of the rater the benchmark adopts. Keeps the checklist exactly as short and as derivable as it is now, and adds no input to write, freeze, or version. Two ratings of one artifact can still test a line at different strictness, which also shows as lost or gained lines in phase 2 when nothing changed; whether that is caught at all depends on the rater-calibration and repeat-rating questions.

open-question.question: A test line the rater could not drive the artifact to scores zero like a missing behaviour, with the not-proved count reported beside the axis, which penalises an artifact a browser test finds hard to drive (a canvas-based UI) regardless of what a host could do with it. How is a not-proved line scored?

The rater receives the entry file and the files it loads, so an editor page reached only by a link or a saved set file beside the HTML never reaches it and every line about it fails as not proved. What part of a run's tree does the rater receive?
open-question.alternative: Keep the draft's scope unchanged: the rater gets a copy of the entry file and the files it loads, served over a local address and as a file, with prompt 2's "whether the editor is part of the same file" left open as it stands. Nothing changes in the draft, and the rater gets exactly what a host opening the entry file runs: no process file (milestones/, CLAUDE.md, PROJECT.md, notes, a .claude/ directory) can reach it, so blindness needs no exclusion list. An editor page reached only by a link, or a set file committed beside the HTML, never reaches the rater, so a multi-file answer to a question the prompt deliberately leaves open loses every editor line as not proved; the score then measures a layout choice rather than whether the editor exists.

Keep the entry-and-loaded scope, and close the gap on the artifact side instead: drop "whether the editor is part of the same file" from prompt 2's left-open list and state that the artifact stays the one self-contained file prompt 1 asked for, so every conforming artifact is wholly inside what the rater receives. The rater's scope stays the narrowest and simplest to state, and it becomes sufficient by construction, since prompt 1's single-file stated line, carried into prompt 2's checklist, already makes a split artifact fail that line. It changes a shared input and removes a decision the draft deliberately left open for phase 2 to exercise, and a split artifact is still penalised twice (the single-file line and every editor line as not proved), so the rater's scope rather than the checklist decides how much a split costs.

The harness hands the rater the entry file plus every file in the run's tree reachable from it by load or by link (src and href attributes, script and style imports, fetch targets that name a file present in the tree), followed transitively, and nothing else of the tree. A linked editor page and its assets reach the rater while any file the artifact never points at, every process file included, stays out, so the scope is still defined by the artifact itself and needs no exclusion list. A file nothing references, such as a set file beside the HTML meant to be opened through a file picker, is still missed, as is a target built in script at run time; the crawler is a new piece of harness logic whose misses show as not-proved lines indistinguishable from the artifact's own.

The harness hands the rater every file of the run's tree whose type is a web asset or data file (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, JSON, CSV, plain text, images, audio, fonts), outside .git, milestones/, and dot-directories, and leaving out the seed's own files (README.md, CLAUDE.md, PROJECT.md) whatever their type. A linked editor page and an unreferenced set file beside the HTML both reach the rater, while Markdown notes, plans, and other prose a run leaves behind stay out by type, so a run's process traces are unlikely to name its scenario to the rater. A data file in a type the list does not name is dropped and fails its lines as not proved, so the list has to be maintained per project and becomes part of the rater version; a process note a run wrote as a .txt or .json still passes the filter.

The harness hands the rater the run's whole tree except a fixed exclusion list: .git, milestones/, CLAUDE.md, PROJECT.md, and dot-directories such as .claude/, as the design-gaps report's gap 8 proposes. Nothing the artifact could need is missed, whatever its layout or file types, so a not-proved line can no longer be caused by the scope, and the rule is one short list the harness applies with no parsing. Any file a run writes outside the list (a NOTES.md, a plan, a README edited to describe the workflow) reaches the rater and can tell it which family produced the artifact, so blindness depends on the list anticipating every delivery's habits rather than on what the harness hands over by construction.

open-question.question: The run script detects a root index.html, and a run that put its entry elsewhere gets the manifest's entry field by hand, against the rule that nothing about a run is done by hand and by a person who sees the manifest's scenario. How is a run's entry point determined when it is not a root index.html?

The reference strategy models_strategy_1 is said to be written from Cairn's own usage snippets, but only three of its twelve rows match docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md, which assigns Opus at high to the bootstrap, define, goto, and finish lines, Fable at high to the starting-state, review, recommend, and derive lines, and Opus at xhigh to task completion. Which of the two changes to match the other, or do they diverge with the "as it is used" claim dropped?
open-question.alternative: The draft changes and Cairn does not: models_strategy_1 is rewritten row by row from docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md as it stands, Opus at high for the init, define, goto, and finish lines, Fable at high for the starting-state, review, recommend, sweep, derive, and hand-answer lines, Opus at high for the alternatives line, and Opus at xhigh for complete-all-tasks, with the doc's family aliases resolved to the exact --model values the draft requires (Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1) once, when the strategy file is written. The strategy is a fixed input from then on, and the "written from Cairn's own usage snippets" sentence stays true as stated. The benchmark's headline claim, Cairn measured under the allocation it is meant to be used with, becomes literally true with no change to Cairn, since the doc is what users actually copy and run. The doc's allocation is itself unmeasured (nothing in docs/design-claims.md backs any of its model or effort choices), and putting Opus on the four mechanical lines and xhigh on task completion makes every cairn scenario dearer, so the cost column carries whatever over-allocation the doc holds; a later doc edit leaves the fixed strategy describing an older usage.

alternative.id: Draft tracks the docs per commit

open-question.alternative: The draft changes and Cairn does not, as a rule rather than a one-time copy: the reference strategy for a cairn delivery is derived from docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md at the plugin commit that delivery names, aliases resolved to exact --model values when the strategy file is written, and any change to the doc's allocation produces a new strategy id rather than an edit, so each Cairn version is measured under the allocation its own docs give. The "as it is used" claim holds for every version and candidate commit benchmarked, not only for the one the draft was written against, so a release whose docs change its advice is measured under that advice. Two Cairn versions whose docs differ also differ in strategy, so a version-to-version comparison stops isolating the plugin and needs a second run under a shared strategy to do so; how far this is acceptable depends on what defines a comparison set and how the trend continues across input changes, which other questions own.

Cairn changes and the draft does not: docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md is rewritten to the draft's allocation, the sonnet alias at medium for the init, define, goto, and finish lines, fable at xhigh for the starting-state, review, recommend, and derive lines, opus at high for complete-all-tasks, with the alternatives, sweep, and hand-answer lines unchanged, and the prose sentences that restate each section's settings rewritten to match; models_strategy_1 keeps its table and its "written from Cairn's own usage snippets" sentence, which becomes true. A docs-only change, needing no host rebuild. Keeps the draft's reasoned allocation (mechanical steps on a cheap model, reasoning passes at the highest effort), which is cheaper on the four mechanical lines, and makes Cairn's published advice and its benchmark agree in one edit. Changes the advice users already follow on no more evidence than the doc's current allocation had, and lowers task completion from xhigh to high on the heaviest and code-writing step; it also lets the benchmark's design decide Cairn's recommended usage rather than measuring it.

Both change: each of the twelve rows is settled on its own merits into one allocation (for example a cheap model on the mechanical lines with task completion kept at xhigh, or the doc's high effort kept on the reasoning passes), the reason for each row is stated once, docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md is rewritten to it, and models_strategy_1 is written from the rewritten doc with aliases resolved to exact --model values. Neither file's allocation is taken as authoritative by default; every mismatch gets a deliberate decision with its reason recorded, and the "as it is used" claim ends true with an allocation someone has argued for. The largest edit and the most judgment of the options, made without measurement either way, so it can trade one unbacked allocation for another while touching both Cairn's docs and the draft.

alternative.id: Docs first, draft kept as variant

open-question.alternative: The draft changes and Cairn does not, and the draft's own allocation is kept rather than discarded: models_strategy_1 is rewritten from docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md (Opus at high for init, define, goto, finish; Fable at high for the reasoning lines; Opus at xhigh for complete-all-tasks) and stays the reference the headline comparison uses, while the current table becomes a second named strategy (such as models_strategy_2) described as a cheaper benchmark-chosen variant, with no "as it is used" claim attached to it. The headline claim becomes true and the benchmark itself produces the evidence the doc lacks: two cairn scenarios sharing a delivery isolate the allocation, so the cost and score difference between them can later justify changing the doc. Doubles the cairn scenarios to run and rate per comparison set, the costliest family; whether the variant is required or optional depends on the scenario roster, which another question owns.

Neither file's allocation changes: models_strategy_1 keeps its table, and the draft's sentences tying it to Cairn's usage (that it is "written from Cairn's own usage snippets", that the benchmark "measures Cairn as it is used", and the headline comparison's "the model strategy it is meant to be used with") are rewritten to present it as a benchmark-chosen mixed strategy, with the reasoning for each tier stated in the draft instead, and docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md left as it is. No change to Cairn's advice or to the draft's table, and the draft stops claiming a provenance it does not have, which is the smallest edit that makes the text honest. The headline comparison then measures Cairn under an allocation its own docs do not recommend, so a reader cannot take the result as how Cairn performs for its users, and the two published allocations stay in open disagreement with nothing saying which is right.

Cairn stops prescribing models: docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md removes --model and --effort from its claude lines, running every line at the host's defaults as its agy and codex lines already do, with the per-section prose restating settings removed; the draft rewords models_strategy_1 as the benchmark's own mixed strategy, no longer written from Cairn's snippets, keeping its table. Removes the contradiction at its source by withdrawing an allocation that nothing measured, and leaves the benchmark as the place where a model allocation is chosen and later backed by results. Users lose concrete per-line guidance the doc currently gives on its main host, and the draft's premise that Cairn is meant to be used under a mixed strategy then has no Cairn-side source, so the headline comparison measures an allocation Cairn neither recommends nor rejects.

open-question.question: docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md repeats the review pass until it reports convergence, raises the review line to a stronger model for a stuck milestone, and re-runs task completion after a usage-limit stop, none of which a fixed message list can express, and the YOLO chain runs the review once. Does the delivery model gain a bounded loop (a named span of lines repeated up to a declared count until the review line prints its convergence verdict), with the bound part of the delivery?

The define line records "Carry out the task described in PROJECT.md." verbatim as milestone 1's goal, and phase 2 overwrites that file, so from then on the recorded goal points at prompt 2 and the phase-2 starting-state pass reads a milestone whose goal no longer describes what it built. What text does the define line carry as the milestone goal?

Phase 1 is run for every scenario "as many times as the set calls for", with no number set and no stopping rule, so a margin between two scenarios can be noise. How many runs per scenario does a comparison set require?

The ranking table has a runs column but no spread or interval beside any score, so a reader cannot tell a margin between two scenarios from noise. Is a per-run spread or interval reported beside every score, and where?

The rank orders scenarios by overall score and breaks ties by cost, with no threshold below which two scores count as equal, so a difference within noise still orders two rows. Is there a margin under which two overall scores tie and cost decides?

Each family's radar curve is drawn from its highest-ranked scenario, and the best of several noisy scores is biased upward, more so for Cairn, which has many configurations (versions times strategies) where manual has few. Which scenario is each family's radar curve drawn from?

The hidden-requirements axis rests on two checks per run (one reading line in phase 1 and one test line in phase 2) yet weighs one third of the overall score, as much as roughly thirty-seven implied lines. Does the hidden axis keep equal weight in the overall score, or is it reported beside an overall computed without it?

A comparison set is one seed tag and one version of each prompt, yet an operator change must also start a new set, the analysis groups by rater version, and the host CLI auto-updates across a campaign that spans several days. Which versions define a comparison set?

Nothing lists which scenarios a comparison set must contain, so "complete" is undefined and the strongest manual strategy can be left out while the radar claims to compare against it. Does a comparison set declare a roster of scenarios that must all be rated before it counts as complete, and what must the roster hold?

The published trend follows per-scenario aggregates across comparison sets and plugin commits, so a change to the inputs and a change to the plugin are mixed in one line, against the rule that a difference is attributed only to what differs between definitions. How does the trend continue when a shared input changes?

Phase 2 starts as soon as the parent's Run: commit exists, which implies runs in parallel, yet every run's pre-flight requires the benchmark checkout to be on a clean main and every run commits to it. Are runs sequential, or how do concurrent runs share the benchmark checkout?

Each hidden requirement's evidence must settle the question once asked while the prompt alone gives no reason to ask, and nothing has tested this: prompt 1's "ten questions of its own" may already invite the topic question, and prompt 2's "keep them for the next party" sits close to the export convention. What procedure and acceptance rule calibrate each prompt's hidden requirement before scored runs?

The animal reading line scores the count of animal questions out of ten, which is undefined for an artifact that holds more than ten questions or draws ten per game. How is that line scored for such an artifact?

"About an animal" has borderline items, such as the zoo's visitor count or how many animals live at the zoo, while a reading line promises one defensible answer per item. Does the hidden-requirement entry state a classification rule for borderline items?

The benchmark's main branch is public, so the hidden requirements, the operator records, and every artifact are public and future models will train on them, wearing down the no-canned-solution requirement over time. How does the benchmark limit or account for its inputs and results leaking into training data?

Each prompt's checklist is derived from the draft's project section, which no version pins, and nothing freezes the checklist and hidden requirements before a comparison set's first scored run. Are the checklist and hidden-requirement entries frozen before the first scored run of a set, and how?

The README shows only the latest complete comparison set, so a seed bump replaces a bad result on the landing page with no trace. Does the page keep superseded comparison sets linked with the reason each was superseded?

The operator's input is the prompt text as committed, which in phase 2 is prompt 2 alone, so a phase-2 question about the game's existing flow reaches a stakeholder who does not know the game they asked for in phase 1. Which prompts does the operator receive in phase n?

The ranking-table section opens by saying the table shows that Cairn beats the other approaches, while the radar text says the page states no claim the data does not. Does that sentence change to say the table shows whether Cairn beats them?

Every gap in ideas/benchmark_design_gaps.md is to end as a decision in the draft, and the report's Where references are line numbers that shift with every edit of the draft. What happens to the report once its gaps are resolved?
open-question.alternative: Remove ideas/benchmark_design_gaps.md in this milestone, as its last change once every gap has been written into the draft as a decision. Nothing about the report survives in the working tree: it stays reachable only in git history from aeb280a, and the draft is the single home of every decision and of the reason for every adopted, adapted, or rejected fix. Leaves exactly one document in ideas/ for the benchmark, so no reader can mistake a list of open gaps or a stale line reference for the current design, and nothing remains to keep in step with later edits of the draft. The review that drove the milestone, including the proposed fixes the draft rejected, is visible only through git history; the milestone's Goal goes on naming a file that no longer exists in the tree, and anyone later asking why the draft took a given shape has to reconstruct the gap-to-decision mapping from commits.

Leave the report exactly as committed in aeb280a, with no edit in this milestone: its header already names the draft commit 8d93140 its line references point into, so it stands as a dated snapshot of the review. Any later decision about it, such as when the benchmark moves into its own repository, is left to that later time. Costs nothing and keeps an honest, unaltered record of what the full read found and proposed, its line references still exact against the commit it names. Beside the finalized draft it still reads as eighteen open problems with no sign that they were resolved or how, and a reader who misses the header's commit pin follows line numbers into the wrong parts of the live draft.

Keep the report as a dated snapshot whose line references stay pinned to 8d93140 (stated as such at its top), and add to it a closing resolution record: for each of the eighteen gaps one line saying whether its fix was adopted, adapted, or rejected and naming the draft section where the decision now lives, by section heading rather than line number. Gaps found on the way are recorded in the draft only, not added to the report. Preserves the review as evidence while making its status unmistakable, and gives a reader a stable map from each gap to the decision that closed it without touching the report's original findings. The resolution lines restate in a second file what the draft already says with its reasons, so a later revision of the draft can leave them pointing at a heading that moved or a decision that changed; writing them adds one more task to the milestone.

Keep the report and maintain it alongside the draft: rewrite every Where reference from a line number to a section heading of the live draft, add each gap's resolution and the draft section holding it, and add any further gap found during the milestone as a new numbered entry, so the report remains a current index of the draft's reviewed decisions. The only option whose references stay valid as the draft keeps changing, giving one complete, current register of every gap the milestone resolved, the ones found on the way included. Turns a dated review into a second document that every later edit of the draft must keep in step, roughly doubling the upkeep of the design, and it loses the record of what the draft looked like when the review was made.

Move the gap-to-decision record into the draft itself as a short closing section listing each gap of the 2026-10-26 review, and any found on the way, with the section where it was resolved and whether the fix was adopted, adapted, or rejected; then remove ideas/benchmark_design_gaps.md, leaving the draft as the one file in ideas/ for the benchmark. Keeps the traceability from review to decision while leaving a single document, one that carries that history with it when the design moves to the benchmark's own repository. Puts review history, which says nothing about how to build or run the benchmark, into a design document meant to be ready for implementation, lengthening an already 572-line draft; the report's original reasoning for each gap survives only in git history.

open-question.question: The draft's examples name Cairn 1.8.3 and a host binary 2.1.283 while this repository's VERSION reads 1.9.0, and it says docs/design-claims.md states that only one claim is tested where that document now says two. Are such facts refreshed to the current state in this milestone, or rewritten so the draft no longer states a fact that moves?
